## Ecommerce Website Development in Pune: Shopify or WooCommerce? How to Choose the Right Platform for Your Store

Choose Shopify if you want a hosted store that someone without a developer can run, and you are happy to work inside its rules. Choose WooCommerce if you want to own the code and server, need unusual customisation, and have a developer or agency who will look after it. That is the short answer, and it is right more often than not. The real decision is less about features, because both platforms can sell almost anything, and more about **who carries the responsibility** for speed, security, updates and fixes after launch. This guide is for owners and managers weighing ecommerce website development in Pune who want a way to decide, not a verdict that suits whoever is selling the build.

We do not repeat the fee comparison here. Gateway charges and platform transaction fees are covered in our guide to [Shopify and WooCommerce payment gateway fees](/blog/shopify-woocommerce-payment-gateway-fees/), and we avoid quoting rates that change often. Where we mention a price, we say when it was checked, and where a figure could not be confirmed we say so.

### How to use this article

Read the first three sections to understand what actually differs. Then use the decision questions and the hypothetical example to test your own situation. The comparison table and the "when neither fits" section help if your needs are unusual. If you would rather talk it through, the closing section says how.

## The real difference: hosted store versus software you run

Shopify is a hosted service. You pay a monthly plan, Shopify runs the servers, applies security updates and keeps the checkout online. You configure the store, choose a theme, add apps, and work within what the platform allows.

WooCommerce is a free, open-source plugin that turns a WordPress site into a store. The software costs nothing to download, but you must host it somewhere and keep it updated. WooCommerce publishes its own server requirements: for WooCommerce 10.8 and later, WordPress 6.9 or newer, PHP 8.3 or newer (tested up to 8.4), MySQL 8.0 or newer or MariaDB 10.6 or newer, HTTPS, and a memory limit of at least 256 MB. It also notes a legacy path for hosts running older software and warns those versions have reached end of life and may expose the site to vulnerabilities ([WooCommerce server requirements](https://woocommerce.com/document/server-requirements/)). A shared hosting plan that cannot meet those numbers is not a bargain for a store.

Everything else follows from that split.

- **Responsibility.** On Shopify, uptime and platform security are Shopify's problem. On WooCommerce they are yours, or your agency's.
- **Freedom.** On Shopify you customise within boundaries. On WooCommerce you can change nearly anything, including things you should not.
- **Cost shape.** Shopify is a predictable subscription plus apps. WooCommerce is lower rent but variable spend on hosting, plugins and developer hours.

Neither is "cheaper" in the abstract. A WooCommerce store with no maintenance budget is cheap until it breaks. A Shopify store with ten paid apps is simple until the invoices add up.

## Seven questions that decide it

### 1. Who will run the store day to day?

If the person managing products, orders and offers is a business owner or an operations executive with no technical help, Shopify's admin is built for them. Adding products, editing collections, changing a banner and processing orders are all done in one dashboard, with the platform handling the rest.

WooCommerce's admin is also usable by non-technical staff for daily tasks. The difference shows up when something goes wrong: a plugin conflict after an update, a slow checkout, an email that stops sending. Those need someone with access to the server and the code. Ask honestly who that person is. If the answer is "the agency, on a maintenance plan", WooCommerce works well. If the answer is "nobody", lean to Shopify.

### 2. How big and how complicated is the catalogue?

A few dozen to a few thousand products with ordinary variants such as size and colour suit either platform. Pressure appears at the edges.

- **Many options per product.** If a product has several independent options and many combinations, check the platform's limits before you design around them. Shopify documents its variant behaviour in its help centre ([Shopify product variants](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/products/details/product-variants)); confirm the current limits there, since they change, and TODO: verify the exact figures against your own catalogue before committing.
- **Made-to-order or configurable products.** Engraving, stitching measurements or bundled kits are possible on both, but WooCommerce plugins and custom code tend to give more control over the product page. On Shopify this usually means an app or theme work.
- **Large or messy imports.** Both support CSV imports. The harder problem is data quality, which we cover in our guide to [preparing product catalogue data](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-product-catalogue-data-preparation-2026/).

### 3. How much customisation do you genuinely need?

Be specific. "A unique look" is a design task and both platforms can do it. "A checkout that behaves differently for wholesale buyers" is a logic task, and platforms differ.

On Shopify, checkout customisation is deliberately controlled. Shopify's help centre states that standard checkout customisations are available on the Basic plan or higher, while advanced customisation, such as apps on the information, shipping and payment pages and the Checkout Branding API, is available only on Shopify Plus ([Shopify checkout settings](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/checkout-settings/checkout-extensibility)). Plus starts at a published price in the lakhs of rupees per month (see the pricing page), so a requirement that forces Plus changes the economics.

On WooCommerce the checkout is code you control. That is a strength if you need custom fields, rules or flows, and a risk if each change adds something to maintain. If your checkout needs are unusual, read our overview of [building a checkout system](/services/checkout-system) before choosing.

### 4. Where do your performance and security responsibilities sit?

A store that loads slowly loses buyers, and Google measures loading, responsiveness and layout stability through Core Web Vitals. On Shopify, the platform's servers and CDN are managed for you, but your theme and apps still decide how heavy each page is. On WooCommerce, you are also choosing hosting, caching and the database setup. Neither platform protects you from fifteen scripts on every page.

For the details, see our guide to [store speed and Core Web Vitals for ecommerce](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-store-speed-core-web-vitals-2026/). The practical point is that "managed" and "unmanaged" describe who handles the server, not who is responsible for a fast storefront.

On security, a hosted platform removes server patching from your list. A self-hosted store keeps it on the list permanently: WordPress core, WooCommerce, the theme, every plugin and the PHP version all need updating. That is routine work for a developer and a neglected chore for everyone else.

### 5. What do Indian buyers and Indian operations need?

This is where a generic "Shopify vs WooCommerce" article from another country misleads. For an Indian store, check these before you commit.

- **Payment gateways.** Both platforms connect to Indian gateways, but the integration route differs. Shopify's pricing page lists a third-party gateway transaction fee on each plan, and states that Shopify Payments is available only in certain countries ([Shopify pricing](https://www.shopify.com/in/pricing)). WooCommerce charges no platform fee on orders, but you rely on the gateway's plugin. Our [payment gateway integration service](/services/payment-gateway) page describes what we check on either route.
- **Cash on delivery.** COD is a major part of many Indian stores. Both platforms can handle it, usually through plugin or app configuration. The real work is order verification and RTO handling, which sits outside this comparison.
- **GST invoices.** Invoices with GSTIN, HSN codes and tax lines are a build task on either platform, typically through an app, plugin or custom template. Confirm that your chosen route produces invoices your accountant accepts before launch.
- **WhatsApp.** Order updates and customer messages over WhatsApp are common. Both platforms connect to WhatsApp providers through apps, plugins or custom integration. See [WhatsApp commerce](/whatsapp/commerce) and our guide to [WhatsApp Business API for ecommerce websites](/blog/whatsapp-business-api-ecommerce-website-pune-2026/).
- **Shipping.** Courier and aggregator integrations exist for both. If you need a custom shipping flow, our [logistics integration](/services/logistic-integration) page is the place to start.
- **Regional languages.** If you plan Marathi or Hindi storefronts, check how each platform's theme and translation tools handle them.

None of these rules out either platform. They tell you what to test in a demo.

### 6. How locked in will you be?

Switching platforms later is possible on both sides but never free. A product and customer export is usually straightforward; order history, URLs, reviews, apps' data and custom logic are harder.

- **Shopify.** You can export core data, but your theme code, app configurations and some app data stay with the platform or the app vendor. Ask what you can export, in what format, and what you would lose.
- **WooCommerce.** Your data lives in your own database and files, so you can move hosts or agencies without asking anyone's permission, as long as your agency has handed over access. Our [website handover and ownership checklist](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-handover-ownership-checklist-2026/) lists what you should hold.

The honest framing: WooCommerce gives you easier ownership of the data and code, Shopify gives you less to look after. Which of those matters more depends on how much you value control compared with convenience.

### 7. What does the next two years look like?

If you plan to add wholesale pricing, subscriptions, marketplaces, multiple storefronts, an app or integrations with an ERP, think about which platform makes those easier. Shopify has an app ecosystem for many of these needs, at monthly cost. WooCommerce has plugins and the freedom to build custom features, at development cost. If you expect heavy customisation, cost out the custom route now instead of discovering it in year two.

## Shopify and WooCommerce compared

| Question | Shopify | WooCommerce |
|---|---|---|
| Who hosts it | Shopify | You, or a host you choose |
| Platform cost | Monthly plan; check current INR prices on Shopify's pricing page | Software is free; you pay for hosting, plugins and developer time |
| Platform fee on third-party gateway orders | Yes, listed per plan on Shopify's pricing page | None from the platform; gateway charges apply |
| Updates and security patches | Platform handles core | You handle core, plugins, theme and PHP |
| Checkout customisation | Standard on Basic and above; advanced on Plus only, per Shopify's help centre | Full control, with code to maintain |
| Add-on cost | App subscriptions | Plugin licences and custom development |
| Data ownership | Exports available; theme and some app data stay in the ecosystem | Data and files in your own hosting |
| Best fit | Non-technical teams, quick launch, predictable operations | Teams with a developer, unusual requirements, content-heavy stores |
| Main risk | Many apps adding cost and page weight; Plus required for deep checkout changes | Neglected updates, weak hosting, plugin conflicts |

Prices change. As seen on Shopify's India pricing page when this article was prepared, Basic, Grow and Advanced were listed at different monthly prices depending on whether billing was yearly or monthly, with third-party gateway fees of 2%, 1% and 0.6% respectively, and Plus starting in the lakhs per month. Check the live page before budgeting, because plan names, prices and fees are revised.

## A hypothetical example: three stores, three answers

The following are invented for illustration. They are not clients, and the numbers are deliberately not given.

**Store A: a founder selling handmade skincare, 60 products, one person handling orders.** No technical help, a need to launch quickly, and ordinary variants. Shopify fits: the owner can manage the store alone, and the monthly fee is the price of not needing a developer on call. The watch-out is app creep, so the brief should limit which apps are added and why.

**Store B: a regional distributor with 4,000 products, customer-specific price lists and a need to push orders to an accounting system.** Complex pricing and integration logic. WooCommerce, with a developer on a maintenance plan, gives room to build the pricing rules and integration. If the team has no ongoing developer, the same requirements could force Shopify Plus, which changes the cost picture. It is worth costing both routes. Our guide to [wholesale and trade-pricing ordering](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-wholesale-b2b-ordering-trade-pricing-2026/) covers this kind of store.

**Store C: a content-led store with a large blog, buying guides and product pages that rank in search.** WordPress is strong at content, so WooCommerce keeps store and content in one system. Shopify has blogging, but if the content engine is the core of acquisition, the content tooling should weigh in the decision. Either way, plan the structure with the help of our [SEO service](/services/seo) approach rather than leaving it to the theme.

The point of the three examples: the same two platforms give different answers because the teams, catalogues and growth plans differ.

## What the first year really includes

A platform choice is a commitment to a list of recurring tasks. Write that list down before you decide.

**On Shopify, expect:**
- reviewing app subscriptions every quarter and removing those that are unused;
- keeping theme and app changes tested, because apps inject code into your storefront;
- checking the checkout and thank-you page after any app or theme change;
- monitoring storefront speed, since the platform's servers are not the only factor.

**On WooCommerce, expect:**
- updating WordPress, WooCommerce, the theme and every plugin on a schedule, after testing on a staging copy;
- keeping PHP and the database on supported versions, as the WooCommerce requirements page states;
- backups that have been restored at least once, as we describe in our [website backups and recovery guide](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-backups-disaster-recovery-2026/);
- hosting that matches the store's traffic, and an owner for security monitoring.

If your team cannot name who does each task, that is more important than any feature table.

## When neither platform fits

Sometimes the honest answer is neither.

- **A very simple catalogue.** A dozen products that rarely change may be served well by a modest site with a WhatsApp order flow, as long as you understand the limits: no stock management, manual order handling and weaker tracking.
- **Highly custom business logic.** Rental, booking, auction or multi-vendor models may justify a custom build. This costs more upfront and needs long-term ownership, but you avoid forcing a product-shaped platform to do something it was not designed for.
- **Performance- or experience-led brands that want full control of the front end.** A headless setup separates the storefront from the commerce back end. It adds engineering and maintenance work, and it is not a shortcut. Our [headless commerce guide](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-headless-commerce-2026/) explains when it is worth it.

A good agency should tell you if a platform is wrong for you, even if that means a smaller project.

## Questions to ask any agency before you sign

These work for any ecommerce website development company in Pune, including us.

1. Which platform do you recommend for my store, and what would change your recommendation?
2. Who will own the hosting, domain, platform and app accounts, and in whose name are they?
3. What is included in launch, and what is excluded: product upload, GST invoices, COD, shipping integration, redirects from the old site?
4. What will I pay each month after launch, split by platform, apps or plugins, hosting and maintenance?
5. How will updates be tested before reaching the live store?
6. What will be done if the store breaks on a Saturday night?
7. What do I receive at handover: logins, code, documentation, backups?
8. Show me a store you built on this platform that is live and measured, and what its owner maintains themselves.

If answers are vague, treat that as information. Pair this list with the checks in our [pre-launch testing checklist](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-pre-launch-testing-checklist-2026/).

## A simple decision path

1. List your must-haves: payment methods, COD, GST invoices, languages, integrations, special pricing.
2. Write down who will run daily operations and who will fix technical problems.
3. Cost both routes for twelve months, including apps or plugins, hosting and developer time. Use ranges and label unknowns as unknown.
4. Check the one or two requirements that could break the choice, such as a checkout rule that forces Shopify Plus or a hosting need that WooCommerce cannot meet affordably.
5. Ask an agency to prototype the riskiest requirement on your preferred platform before you commit to the full build.
6. Decide, and write down the reason, so you can revisit it when your business changes.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Shopify or WooCommerce better for a small business in India?

It depends on who will run the store. Shopify suits owners who want a hosted store with no server work, while WooCommerce suits businesses with a developer who can host, update and customise it. Compare twelve-month total cost, not just the monthly platform price.

### Is WooCommerce really free?

The WooCommerce plugin is free to download, but running a store needs hosting that meets its server requirements, plus a theme, plugins as needed, payment gateway charges and maintenance. WooCommerce's own documentation lists current server requirements, so check your host against them.

### Can I switch from Shopify to WooCommerce, or the other way, later?

Yes, but it takes planning. Products and customers can be exported and imported, while order history, URLs, reviews, theme code and app data need individual handling. Set up redirects from old URLs to new ones so search traffic is not lost.

### Does Shopify work for Indian payments and cash on delivery?

Shopify connects to Indian payment gateways through third-party integrations and can offer COD through apps or configuration. Its pricing page lists a fee on third-party gateway orders per plan and notes Shopify Payments is available only in certain countries, so confirm your payment route and its fees before you build.

Sources: [Shopify India pricing](https://www.shopify.com/in/pricing); [Shopify help centre: checkout settings](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/checkout-settings/checkout-extensibility); [Shopify help centre: product variants](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/products/details/product-variants); [WooCommerce server requirements](https://woocommerce.com/document/server-requirements/).
